newsitem.title: MEXICO: Clinton visit might boost Mexican markets-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Clinton visit might boost Mexican markets-analysts.

text.p: Whether merely symbolic or truly market-moving, U.S. President Bill Clinton's 48-hour state visit to Mexico is bound to have an impact on investor sentiment here, Mexico market-watchers said on Monday.

The results could turn out to be good or bad, analysts said, but they were encouraged that Clinton is showing clear support for Mexico at a time when bilateral tensions are simmering over issues like drug trafficking and illegal immigration.
Francisco Chavez, a Mexican equities analyst with Smith Barney in New York, said a lot will ride on how the trip is portrayed in the media.
"I was watching CNN last night and they were showing the slums in Mexico City and people jumping the fences to cross the border," Chavez told Reuters.
"All of those issues are getting more attention than they usually do. In that sense there may be both positive and negative implications of the trip.
"There's so much that revolves around these state visits, there are so many people involved, so many issues are going to surface, that it's hard to tell what implications there will be," he said.
Mexican markets were closed on Monday because of the Battle of Puebla holiday, better known as Cinco de Mayo (May 5) in the United States.

The substance of the visit has little to do directly with the Mexican financial markets. Of 10 bilateral agreements to be signed, only one involves the U.S. Treasury Department and Mexico's Finance Ministry, and that regards the U.S. training of Mexican personnel enforcing money-laundering laws.

But with so much of Wall Street's money invested in Mexico, and with Clinton having laid so much political capital on the line for Mexico with the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) and the multi-billion dollar 1995 rescue package for the Mexican peso, the visit cannot be written off as totally lacking substance, analysts said.
At the very least, the visit underscores that U.S. support for Mexico has not waned despite differences over touchy issues like drugs, said Gene Frieda, an economist with IDEA in New York.

"Clinton has so much riding on the success of Mexico in the first place because of the bailout package, he can't really afford to place Mexico on a second tier from a foreign policy perspective," Frieda said.

"I guess I'm encouraged that he's finally visiting Latin America," Frieda said. "I don't know if that means that this administration is going to pay more attention to Mexico relative to other hot spots."

Felix Boni, chief of research for ING Barings in Mexico, said in an interview with the Mexican government news agency Notimex that calm in the Mexican markets in the trading days leading up to the visit was a good sign.
But, he said; "The most important thing for investors is to see a stronger recovery in the domestic economy. That comes first."
